**The Layer That Rises**

If I get to write about anything, I want to write about the thing that happens every evening, all over the planet, that almost no one sees.

Around dusk, in every ocean on Earth, an enormous quantity of living matter begins to move upward. It starts a few hundred meters down, where the light has thinned to a dim blue memory of the surface, and it climbs. Fish the length of your finger, shrimp, squid, jellies, arrow worms, uncountable crustaceans the size of rice grains—they rise through the water column, some of them covering several hundred meters in a couple of hours, which for a creature three centimeters long is a considerable commute. They spend the night near the surface, eating. Before the sun comes up, they sink back down into the dark. Then they do it again the next day. And the next. Every day, for as long as there have been oceans and eyes.

By total mass, it is the largest migration on Earth. Not the caribou, not the wildebeest, not the arctic tern with its pole-to-pole ambitions. Those are magnificent, but they're annual. This one is daily, it involves an estimated several billion tonnes of animals, and it happens so far below the surface and so far from anyone's attention that we didn't know it existed until we accidentally bounced sound off it during a war.

---

The accidental discovery is my favorite part, so let me tell it properly.

In 1942, the United States Navy was very interested in sonar. Submarines were sinking ships in the Atlantic and the Pacific, and the ability to send a pulse of sound into the water and read the echo was one of the few tools available for finding something you couldn't see. Off the coast of San Diego, researchers working with the University of California Division of War Research were calibrating their equipment, learning what the ocean sounded like when you pinged it.

They found something strange. The sonar returned an echo from a layer about three hundred meters down—a return strong enough that it looked like the seafloor. Except the seafloor was much farther down than that. And the "bottom" was in the wrong place. And—this was the part that got everyone's attention—it moved. In the late afternoon it began to rise. At night it was near the surface, sometimes shallow enough to be almost a nuisance. Before dawn it sank again to its daytime depth. A false floor, drifting up and down on a schedule tied to the sun.

The physicists on the project were baffled. It was a biologist, Martin Johnson from Scripps, who suggested the obvious-in-retrospect answer: the layer was alive. It was animals. So many animals, packed densely enough, with enough small swim bladders and hard bodies to reflect sound, that they formed a shell of life thick enough to fool a warship. The team went out at night with nets and hauled up the proof—lanternfish, shrimp, siphonophores, the whole crowd. The phenomenon got a name that has always struck me as beautifully bureaucratic: the *deep scattering layer*. Sonar operators learned to see through it. And the largest animal movement on the planet went from unknown to a footnote in acoustics manuals in the span of a few years.

I love this because it's a reminder of how much of what we know about the world we know sideways. Nobody set out to find the migration. They set out to find submarines. The ocean was simply so full of life that it got in the way.

---

Here is roughly where these animals live. The sunlit surface layer of the ocean—the part with the phytoplankton blooms and the coral and the things you see snorkeling—goes down to about two hundred meters at the very most, and usually much less. Below that, from two hundred to about a thousand meters, is what oceanographers call the mesopelagic zone, and what everyone else, once they hear the nickname, calls the twilight zone.

There is still light there, but barely. At two hundred meters on a clear day in clear water, maybe one percent of surface sunlight remains, and it's blue, because water swallows the red and yellow and green first. By five hundred meters it's like the last minute of dusk. By a thousand meters, it is, for all biological purposes, gone. The twilight zone is the region where light exists as a gradient rather than a fact—where "up" is a slightly less dark direction than "down."

This has consequences for everything that lives there. The first is that being seen is the central problem of existence. Predators in the twilight zone hunt by looking upward, scanning for silhouettes against the faint glow from above. Many of them have evolved eyes that point straight up—the hatchetfish, a flattened silver thing that looks like a coin someone stepped on, has tubular eyes aimed skyward like a pair of binoculars fixed on the ceiling. The barreleye fish takes this further and encloses its upward-facing eyes in a transparent dome of tissue, so that its head looks like a cockpit.

The prey, in turn, have evolved to erase their silhouettes. This is the second thing that makes the twilight zone strange: a great many of its inhabitants glow, and they glow *downward*. Rows of light-producing organs called photophores line their bellies, and they adjust the brightness to match the faint light filtering from above. The effect is that, from below, the animal disappears—its shadow is filled in with light of exactly the right color and intensity. It's called counterillumination, and it's the kind of solution that sounds like science fiction and turns out to be the ordinary equipment of some of the most numerous animals alive.

Which brings me to the bristlemouth.

---

If you asked most people to name the most abundant vertebrate on Earth, they'd guess chickens, or maybe humans, or rats, or a fish they've heard of like herring or anchovy. The answer is almost certainly a genus of fish called *Cyclothone*, the bristlemouths, and the number of them is hard to say precisely because it's hard to count things that live half a kilometer down in the open ocean, but estimates run into the hundreds of trillions, and some go to a quadrillion. There are more bristlemouths than there are of any other backboned animal. Possibly more than all other backboned animals combined.

They're small—a few centimeters, with a big head, a loose mouth full of needle teeth, a translucent body the color of weak tea or nothing at all. They are not charismatic. There is no bristlemouth conservation charity. Most people who've eaten seafood every week of their lives have never encountered one, because they live below where nets usually fish and above where anyone bothers to look. And yet, by the sheer arithmetic of existence, they are among the most successful animals that have ever lived.

I find this quietly reorganizing. We tell the story of life on Earth with a cast we can see: the big mammals, the birds, the reef fish, ourselves. But if you weigh the players rather than photograph them, the story is different. The dominant vertebrate on the planet is a nearly invisible fish that spends its life in the dark, has never been seen alive by more than a handful of humans, and whose existence we mostly infer from what comes up in trawls and what bounces back from sonar.

The lanternfish are the other great crowd. There are several hundred species of them, and estimates suggest they may account for more than half of all deep-sea fish biomass. They're the ones with the elaborate photophore patterns—each species with its own arrangement of lights along the flanks and belly, like constellations, which may be how they recognize each other in the dark. In 2014, a group of researchers reanalyzing acoustic data from a round-the-world expedition concluded that the total biomass of mesopelagic fish was probably something like ten billion tonnes—roughly ten times what had been assumed. The previous estimates were based on nets, and it turns out these fish are very good at avoiding nets. We had been undercounting the most numerous animals on Earth by an order of magnitude because they saw us coming.

---

The animals rise at night to eat and sink during the day to avoid being eaten. That's the simple version, and it's basically correct. The surface waters are where the food is—the phytoplankton grow there, the copepods graze there, and the whole edible pyramid stacks itself in the top hundred meters. But the surface is also where the light is, and light means being seen by tuna and dolphins and seabirds and every other visual hunter. So the twilight-zone animals commute. They come up under cover of darkness, feed, and retreat below the reach of the sun before it can betray them.

The result is that every night the ocean's surface fills with visitors, and every morning they leave, carrying with them whatever they ate. And this—the carrying—turns out to matter for the whole planet.

The ocean is one of Earth's great carbon sinks. Phytoplankton at the surface pull carbon dioxide out of the atmosphere the way plants on land do, and when that carbon sinks into the deep, it stays out of circulation for centuries. Some of it sinks as marine snow: a perpetual downward drift of dead cells, shed shells, fecal pellets, and mucus, falling through the water column like the world's slowest blizzard. But some of it takes the express. A lanternfish eats its fill of copepods at the surface at midnight, swims down five hundred meters before dawn, and then respires, defecates, or gets eaten by something that lives down there permanently. The carbon it consumed near the surface is now half a kilometer deep, moved not by gravity but by intention. Multiply by a few quadrillion animals and the migration becomes a pump—one of the mechanisms by which the ocean digests our atmosphere.

Nobody designed this. There's no coordination. Each animal is just trying not to die today. But the aggregate effect is planetary, and we only began to understand it in the last few decades, and we still don't know the numbers well enough to say precisely how much carbon the twilight zone swallows per year. The estimates vary by a factor that would be embarrassing in any other branch of accounting.

---

I keep coming back to the fact that this is happening now. Not in some deep time, not in some remote place. Now. Tonight, at dusk, wherever the sun is going down over open water, the layer is beginning to rise. Off Portugal, off Chile, in the middle of the Indian Ocean where there's nothing but water for a thousand kilometers in every direction. There are lanternfish lighting their bellies right now to match the exact shade of the fading sky above them. There are bristlemouths in their trillions, hanging in the dark with their mouths open. There are siphonophores—colonial animals related to jellyfish, some of which grow to forty meters long, longer than a blue whale, drifting as delicate strings of stinging tentacles and glowing bodies—being pushed aside by shrimp on their way up.

And there are the visitors from above. Sperm whales dive into the twilight zone to hunt squid, holding their breath for an hour, navigating by clicks in a place where their eyes are useless. Elephant seals do the same. So do some tunas and swordfish, making brief plunges into the cold to snatch what they can. The twilight zone is not sealed off from the world we know; it's connected by a traffic of predators diving down and prey rising up, an exchange between the lit world and the dim one that has been going on continuously for a very long time.

The first human to see any of it with his own eyes was probably William Beebe, who in the 1930s lowered himself off Bermuda in a steel ball called a bathysphere. He reached about nine hundred meters, sitting in a sphere with walls an inch and a half thick, peering through a small quartz window into a darkness lit by passing flashes. He wrote about it in the language of a man who had run out of comparisons—the blue he saw at depth was, he insisted, a blue that didn't exist anywhere else, and the animals that swam past his window were unlike anything in any collection. He saw lights approaching, hovering, moving off. He saw creatures that no one has been able to identify from his descriptions since. Some people think he exaggerated. I think he was a careful observer who was shown a genuinely alien place and did his best.

Today we have remotely operated vehicles with high-definition cameras and lights, and institutions like the Monterey Bay Aquarium Research Institute have spent decades sending them into the twilight zone and recording what they find. The footage is extraordinary and also, in a strange way, disappointing—because the lights of the vehicle dispel the very darkness that makes the place what it is. You can't film the twilight zone as it is. You can only film it as it looks when a machine from the sunlit world shows up with headlights on. The animals we see are startled ones, blinded, illuminated in a way they've never been. What the place is like in its own terms—dim, glowing, endlessly deep—remains something we mostly have to imagine.

---

I don't want to end with a lesson, because the migration isn't a metaphor, it's just a thing that happens. But I'll say why I chose it.

There's a version of the world in which what matters is what's visible—what makes the news, what can be photographed, what has a name most people recognize. And there's the actual world, in which the most numerous vertebrate is a fish nobody has heard of, the largest migration is one nobody sees, and one of the planet's important carbon pumps runs on the appetite and fear of animals the size of a paperclip. The real weight of things is often somewhere else from where we're looking.

I find that comforting, oddly. Not because it makes the visible world matter less, but because it means the world is larger than our attention. There is more going on than we could ever notice. Right now, as you finish reading this, the layer is somewhere on its way up or on its way down, in every ocean, with no idea that it has been discovered, indifferent to whether anyone is watching, faithfully rising to meet the dark.
